newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says not worried by US-Singapore air pact.
newsitem.headline: Japan says not worried by US-Singapore air pact.

text.p: Japan feels no pressure to move towards an "open-skies" pact with the United States despite a recent accord reached between Washington and Singapore, a Japanese transport ministry said on Friday.
An aviation accord reached between the United States and Singapore on Wednesday will allow airlines from both nations to fly without restrictions to and beyond each other's countries.
It is seen as the first step towards prising open Asia's aviations markets where Japan is regarded as the jewel in the crown.
But Tokyo denies it is under pressure.
"It has no bearing on us whatsoever," the transport ministry official, who declined to be named, told Reuters in an interview. "And the U.S. does not expect Japan to join open skies", he added.
Japan and the United States held exploratory talks on aviation in early January - the first time since formal discussions broke down in August.

Japanese officials said the atmosphere of the talks had greatly improved and that the two sides had agreed to work towards a compromise. Further talks in Washington at an unspecified date in the future are planned.
Tokyo rejects open skies, arguing that such pacts only lead to monopolistic alliances which stifle competition and are dominated by U.S. mega-carriers.
It also argues that the United States should first open its domestic market to foreign carriers.

"Liberalisation begins at home," said the official. Progress, says Tokyo, can only come from redressing imbalances arising from the existing bilateral accord, signed in 1952, which favour U.S. airlines.
U.S. attention shifted to Asia last year after Washington concluded open skies pacts with 12 European countries, including Germany.

That series of separate agreements has been described by analysts as a deliberate building-up of pressure on Britain. The major point of entry to Europe for U.S. carriers, Britain has so far resisted efforts to open its skies, although talks between the two nations have resumed.

These tactics are now being employed against Tokyo, say analysts. The United States plans talks with Malaysia and Taiwan next month and hopes to start talks with South Korea and New Zealand. Talks with Brunei are underway.
Some in the U.S. aviation industry have said, however, that any pressure on Japan is going to be more pyschological than commercial.
"It's not really a direct pressure -- it's really the pressure that comes from being out of step," said Cyril Murphy, United Airlines vice president for international affairs in a recent interview.
Murphy said that for Asian carriers the U.S. market was secondary.
"The biggest and most important is Japan. The ability of the smaller market to put really put pressure on the largest market is somewhat limited," he said. --Tokyo Newsroom + 81-3-3354-0829
